q: A 64-year-old man, Mr Derek Hall, presents to the emergency department with 40 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm, associated with sweating and nausea. He is a smoker with type 2 diabetes. Blood pressure is 148/86 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm. A 12-lead ECG shows 2.5 mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. As you review the ECG you note the blood pressure has fallen to 92/58 mmHg and the jugular venous pressure is elevated, but the lung fields are clear on auscultation. The primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) centre is 45 minutes away and the catheter laboratory has been activated. Which additional ECG lead configuration is most important to obtain before administering nitrates?
options: Repeat leads V1–V6 to look for anterior extension
Lead aVR to assess for left main disease
Modified limb leads (Lewis lead) for atrial activity
explain: This is an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal change in I/aVL) complicated by hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs — the classic triad of right ventricular (RV) infarction. 🫀 Inferior MIs are usually due to right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion, and a proximal RCA lesion can also infarct the RV. RV infarction is preload-dependent: nitrates and other venodilators can precipitate profound hypotension because the failing RV cannot maintain output against a fall in preload. Right-sided chest leads (V3R–V4R) confirm RV involvement — ST elevation ≥1 mm in V4R is highly specific. 🔑 Management pivots on this: avoid nitrates and diuretics, give a cautious fluid bolus to optimise RV preload, and proceed to primary PCI. Recognising RV infarction before reaching for GTN prevents iatrogenic collapse. ESC guidance emphasises right-sided leads in any inferior STEMI with haemodynamic compromise.

q: A 72-year-old woman, Mrs Iris Fenwick, is reviewed in the heart failure clinic. Eight months ago she had an anterior myocardial infarction; a recent echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30%. She remains breathless on moderate exertion (NYHA class II). Her current medication is ramipril 10 mg once daily and bisoprolol 7.5 mg once daily, both at maximally tolerated doses. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 64 bpm and in sinus rhythm. Serum potassium is 4.4 mmol/L and estimated glomerular filtration rate is 62 mL/min/1.73 m². She has no diabetes. According to current ESC heart failure guidance on the four foundational pillars of therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which drug should be added next?
explain: The four pillars of guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF (ESC 2021/2023) are: an ACE inhibitor/ARNI, a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), and an SGLT2 inhibitor. 💊 Mrs Fenwick is already on an ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker at maximal doses. The next foundational agent to add is a MRA — spironolactone (or eplerenone). Her potassium (4.4 mmol/L) and eGFR (62) are within safe limits (K⁺ <5.0 mmol/L and eGFR >30). ✅ The RALES trial (spironolactone) and EMPHASIS-HF (eplerenone) demonstrated clear mortality reduction in HFrEF. An SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin — DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced) is the other missing pillar and would also be appropriate. Ivabradine is only indicated if heart rate remains ≥70 bpm in sinus rhythm despite maximal beta-blockade — her rate is 64. Loop diuretics treat congestion symptomatically but do not improve prognosis.

q: A 78-year-old man, Mr Alan Prentice, is referred with palpitations and breathlessness. An ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 96 bpm. His history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes, a transient ischaemic attack three years ago, and stable angina. Blood pressure is 138/80 mmHg. Renal function is normal (eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73 m²), and he has no history of bleeding. He is already established on amlodipine and metformin. His symptoms are mild and he is keen to avoid hospital admission. Using the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score to guide thromboprophylaxis, what is the most appropriate antithrombotic strategy?
options: Aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy
explain: Mr Prentice's CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is high: hypertension (1), diabetes (1), prior TIA (2), age ≥75 (2), and vascular disease/angina (1) = 7. 🧮 Any score ≥2 in men mandates oral anticoagulation. NICE and ESC now recommend a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban in preference to warfarin for non-valvular AF, given comparable or superior efficacy and lower intracranial bleeding (ARISTOTLE trial for apixaban). ✅ Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF — it is far less effective and carries a similar bleeding risk (this was removed from guidance after the ACTIVE-W and BAFTA data). Dual antiplatelet therapy is inferior to anticoagulation and increases bleeding. His HAS-BLED risk should be assessed, but no absolute contraindication is present. A target INR of 3.0–4.0 is too high and unnecessary — even with warfarin the target is 2.0–3.0. Rate control alone without anticoagulation would leave him at unacceptable stroke risk. 🧠

q: A 58-year-old woman, Mrs Carol Meadows, is admitted with worsening dyspnoea and recurrent presyncope. On examination the JVP is elevated with prominent cannon 'a' waves occurring irregularly. Heart sounds vary in intensity from beat to beat. Her ECG shows a heart rate of 38 bpm; the P waves march out at a regular rate of about 82 per minute, entirely independent of the QRS complexes, which are broad and regular at 38 bpm. Blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg. She takes no rate-limiting drugs and her potassium is 4.1 mmol/L. Troponin is not elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?
options: Oral bisoprolol to suppress the escape rhythm
Overnight observation with telemetry and no intervention
explain: The findings describe complete (third-degree) atrioventricular block: P waves and QRS complexes are entirely dissociated, with atria at ~82/min and a slow, broad ventricular escape at 38/min. 🫀 Cannon 'a' waves (right atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve) occurring irregularly and variable first heart sound intensity are classic physical signs of AV dissociation. She is symptomatic (dyspnoea, presyncope) and haemodynamically borderline. The definitive treatment for symptomatic complete heart block is a permanent pacemaker (NICE/ESC pacing guidance). ⚡ Atropine may be tried acutely but is often ineffective for infranodal (broad-complex) block because the block is below the AV node where vagal tone has little influence — it is a temporising measure, not definitive. Adenosine and beta-blockers would be dangerous, worsening bradycardia. Simple observation is unsafe given her symptoms and risk of asystole. Acute stabilisation may include transcutaneous/transvenous pacing as a bridge, but the correct definitive answer is a permanent pacemaker.

q: A 19-year-old man, Sam Okoye, collapses while playing five-a-side football and is resuscitated after a witnessed cardiac arrest with an initial rhythm of ventricular fibrillation. He recovers fully. There is a family history of sudden cardiac death in a maternal uncle aged 34. On examination there is an ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that becomes louder when he stands from squatting and softer when he squats. The ECG shows deep narrow Q waves in the inferolateral leads and voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy. Echocardiography demonstrates asymmetric septal thickening of 19 mm with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. Which single feature is most strongly associated with his diagnosis and the risk of sudden death?
options: Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction from septal hypertrophy
Fixed subvalvular aortic stenosis due to a membranous shelf
Severe aortic valve calcification with restricted leaflets
Left-to-right shunt through a perimembranous ventricular septal defect
Chordal rupture producing acute mitral regurgitation
explain: This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): young patient, exertional VF arrest, family history of premature sudden death, asymmetric septal hypertrophy (19 mm), and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. 🫀 The murmur behaviour is the key clue: it increases with standing and Valsalva (reduced preload/afterload → smaller LV cavity → worse obstruction) and decreases with squatting (increased venous return → larger cavity → less obstruction). This dynamic character distinguishes HCM from fixed aortic stenosis. ✅ The mechanism of the murmur and of haemodynamic compromise is dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction: the hypertrophied septum narrows the outflow tract, and the high-velocity jet drags the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (Venturi effect → SAM), worsening obstruction and causing mitral regurgitation. HCM is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Risk factors include prior arrest, family history of SCD, unexplained syncope, septal thickness ≥30 mm, and non-sustained VT — informing consideration of an ICD (ESC HCM guidelines). ⚡

q: A 34-year-old man, Mr Tomasz Nowak, who has a history of intravenous drug use, presents with three weeks of fever, night sweats and malaise. Temperature is 38.6°C. There is a soft pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge that increases on inspiration, and small tender nodules are noted on the finger pulps. Chest radiograph shows multiple peripheral cavitating pulmonary lesions. Three sets of blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates a mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve. His C-reactive protein is 180 mg/L and he is haemodynamically stable. Which one of the following, together with the positive blood cultures, best satisfies the modified Duke criteria for a diagnosis of definite infective endocarditis?
options: Fever above 38°C as the second major criterion
Echocardiographic evidence of a valvular vegetation
Peripheral cavitating pulmonary lesions on chest radiograph
A history of intravenous drug use as a major criterion
explain: The modified Duke criteria classify definite infective endocarditis as: 2 major, OR 1 major + 3 minor, OR 5 minor criteria. 🦠 The two major criteria are: 1. Positive blood cultures typical for IE (e.g. persistent bacteraemia with a typical organism such as Staph aureus, viridans streptococci, HACEK, etc.). 2. Evidence of endocardial involvement — a vegetation, abscess or new valvular regurgitation on echocardiography. Mr Nowak has typical positive blood cultures (S. aureus) — one major criterion — and an echocardiographic vegetation on the tricuspid valve — the second major criterion. Two majors = definite IE. ✅ The minor criteria include: predisposition (IVDU, valve disease), fever ≥38°C, vascular phenomena (septic pulmonary infarcts, Janeway lesions), immunological phenomena (Osler's nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis), and microbiological evidence not meeting a major criterion. So IVDU, fever, tender finger nodules (Osler's nodes) and septic pulmonary emboli are all minor criteria — clinically supportive but not the second major criterion here. Right-sided IE with septic pulmonary emboli is classic in IVDU. 💉

q: A 25-year-old woman, Miss Priya Anand, is referred after two episodes of syncope, one occurring while swimming and another triggered by a sudden loud alarm clock. Her brother died suddenly aged 20. She takes no medication other than the combined oral contraceptive pill. Physical examination and echocardiogram are normal. Her resting 12-lead ECG shows a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 520 ms with broad-based, notched T waves. Serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.9 mmol/L and calcium normal. Genetic testing is pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line long-term treatment?
options: Propranolol and avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs
Amiodarone loading followed by maintenance therapy
explain: This is congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS): markedly prolonged QTc (520 ms), broad notched T waves, syncope with adrenergic triggers (swimming, sudden auditory stimulus) and a family history of premature sudden death. ⚡ The triggers point to specific genotypes: swimming/exertion suggests LQT1 (KCNQ1), while sudden auditory stimuli/startle suggests LQT2 (KCNH2). Both are adrenergically driven. First-line therapy is a non-selective beta-blocker — propranolol or nadolol — which blunts the sympathetic surges that precipitate torsades de pointes, combined with strict avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and correction/maintenance of electrolytes. ✅ Nadolol and propranolol are preferred over selective agents. She should also stop any QT-prolonging medication. Sotalol and amiodarone prolong the QT and are contraindicated. Verapamil and flecainide are not first-line (flecainide has a specific niche in LQT3 but is not standard initial therapy). High-risk features (prior cardiac arrest, recurrent syncope on beta-blockade, QTc >500 ms with high-risk genotype) prompt consideration of an ICD (ESC guidance). Left cardiac sympathetic denervation is an adjunct.

q: A 63-year-old man, Mr Geoffrey Watts, is brought in with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back between the shoulder blades. He has poorly controlled hypertension. Blood pressure is 178/98 mmHg in the right arm and 142/80 mmHg in the left arm. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. A CT aortogram confirms a dissection flap involving the ascending aorta and extending to the arch. He is alert and his renal function is normal. Which of the following is the single most appropriate immediate management priority?
options: Intravenous fluid resuscitation to raise blood pressure
Oral amlodipine and outpatient cardiology follow-up
Urgent cardiothoracic surgical referral with intravenous beta-blockade
explain: This is an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection: tearing interscapular pain, an inter-arm blood pressure differential, a new early diastolic murmur (aortic regurgitation from the dissection disrupting the aortic root), a widened mediastinum, and CT confirmation of a flap in the ascending aorta. 🩸 Type A dissections (involving the ascending aorta) are a surgical emergency — untreated mortality is roughly 1–2% per hour in the first 48 hours. The priority is immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral. ⚕️ Alongside this, impulse control is critical: reduce the shearing force (dP/dt) on the aortic wall with intravenous beta-blockade (e.g. labetalol or esmolol), targeting a heart rate <60 bpm and systolic BP ~100–120 mmHg. Beta-blockade should precede vasodilators to avoid reflex tachycardia that would increase wall stress. ✅ Thrombolysis is catastrophic in dissection. Raising the blood pressure with fluids would extend the dissection. Type B (descending only) dissections are usually managed medically, but this is type A and needs surgery. Amlodipine/outpatient follow-up would be fatal.

Raising the blood pressure with fluids would extend the dissection. Type B (descending only) dissections are usually managed medically, but this is type A and needs surgery. Amlodipine/outpatient follow-up would be fatal.

q: A 68-year-old woman, Mrs Doreen Blythe, with atrial fibrillation and mild heart failure is admitted with nausea, anorexia, confusion and disturbed colour vision in which objects appear to have yellow-green haloes. She takes digoxin, furosemide and ramipril. She started a new medication two weeks ago for symptom control. Her ECG shows frequent ventricular ectopics with a bidirectional appearance and the classic 'reverse tick' ST-segment depression. Serum potassium is 3.0 mmol/L, creatinine 148 µmol/L and the serum digoxin concentration is elevated. Which of the following mechanisms best explains why she has developed toxicity at this time?
options: Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 accelerating digoxin metabolism
Increased renal clearance of digoxin from loop diuretic use
Hypokalaemia enhancing digoxin binding to the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Displacement of digoxin from tissue-binding sites raising free levels
explain: Mrs Blythe has classic digoxin toxicity: nausea, anorexia, confusion, xanthopsia (yellow-green visual haloes), bidirectional ventricular ectopy, and the reverse-tick ST depression (which is a sign of digoxin effect, but toxicity is confirmed here by symptoms, arrhythmia and elevated levels). 💛 The crucial mechanism in this case is hypokalaemia (K⁺ 3.0 mmol/L), driven by her furosemide. Digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase by binding to a site on the pump that competes with potassium. When serum potassium is low, there is less competition, so digoxin binds more avidly, potentiating its inhibitory effect and increasing toxicity even at a given serum concentration. ✅ Her worsening renal function (creatinine 148 µmol/L) also reduces digoxin clearance and raises levels, and a newly started drug (e.g. amiodarone or verapamil) may raise digoxin concentrations — but the exam's target mechanism for enhanced toxicity is hypokalaemia increasing pump inhibition. Management: correct potassium and magnesium, stop digoxin, treat arrhythmias, and use digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab) for life-threatening toxicity. ⚕️

q: A 45-year-old man, Mr Idris Bello, presents to the emergency department with sharp central chest pain that is worse on lying flat and relieved by sitting forward. It followed a viral upper respiratory tract illness one week ago. Temperature is 37.8°C. On auscultation there is a scratchy three-component sound at the left sternal edge, best heard on expiration with the patient leaning forward. Blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg with no significant fall on inspiration, and the jugular venous pressure is not elevated. The ECG shows widespread concave ('saddle-shaped') ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression, and PR-segment elevation in lead aVR. Troponin is mildly raised. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
explain: This is acute pericarditis: pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, a preceding viral illness, a pericardial friction rub (scratchy three-component sound), and the classic ECG of widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression plus PR elevation in aVR. The mildly raised troponin suggests some myopericardial involvement (myopericarditis). 🫀 First-line treatment is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) such as ibuprofen (or aspirin) combined with colchicine. The COPE and ICAP trials showed that adding colchicine reduces symptoms and, importantly, recurrence of pericarditis. ✅ (ESC pericardial disease guidelines.) He has no features of tamponade — normal JVP, no pulsus paradoxus, stable BP — so pericardiocentesis is not indicated. There is nothing suggesting bacterial (purulent) pericarditis to warrant antibiotics. Corticosteroids are avoided as first-line because they are associated with a higher recurrence rate; they are reserved for specific causes (e.g. autoimmune) or NSAID-refractory/contraindicated cases. The ECG mimics STEMI but the diffuse concave changes with PR depression and the clinical picture point to pericarditis, not acute coronary occlusion — so primary PCI is not indicated.
